title: Sealing a slate floor with penetrating oil
subtitle: Apply a penetrating impregnator oil to a natural slate floor to protect against stains and moisture without leaving a film on the surface
excerpt: How to seal a natural slate floor with a penetrating oil-based impregnator. Covers cleaning and drying the floor, testing absorbency, applying the oil, buffing the excess, and deciding when to apply a second coat.
sourceNotes: UK natural stone trade practice and stone sealer manufacturer guidance (open access). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: A stone sealer that soaks into the pores of the stone and cures within the surface rather than forming a film on top. It repels water and oil from within while leaving the natural surface appearance and texture intact. Unlike topical sealers, it does not peel, scratch, or trap moisture.

A white powdery deposit on the surface of stone, tile, or masonry caused by soluble salts carried to the surface by moisture and deposited as the water evaporates. On a new slate floor it indicates the floor is still releasing moisture from the screed below: sealing too early traps the salts under the sealer.

content.text: Unsealed slate absorbs oil, water, and stains deeply into the surface. A penetrating impregnator seals from within without leaving a surface film that chips or peels. BEGINNER: clean the floor, apply the oil, and buff the excess. The critical discipline is making sure the floor is completely dry before applying.

Sweep and vacuum to remove all loose grit. Wash the floor with a diluted stone cleaner, scrubbing grout lines with a stiff brush. Rinse with clean water and allow to dry completely before sealing, which typically takes at least two to three days in normal indoor conditions. Check for
: white powdery patches indicate the screed below is still releasing moisture and the floor is not ready to seal.

Drop a small amount of water on the tile surface. If it beads up and stays on the surface for several minutes, the slate has a residual old sealer or natural silica crust: degrease with a specialist stone stripper before applying the new sealer. If the water soaks in within a minute, the stone is open and ready to seal.
Work from the far end of the room toward the door so you do not seal yourself in. Apply the

with a brush or roller in even overlapping strokes, working the product well into the stone and grout lines. Apply enough for the surface to stay visibly wet for two to five minutes, then begin buffing.

Buff the excess sealer from the surface with a clean lint-free cloth or buffing pad before it starts to dry on top of the stone. Any sealer left to dry on the surface will leave a smeared or patchy finish. Once the first coat has dried, typically two to four hours at room temperature, assess absorbency again with a water drop test. If water still soaks in quickly, apply a second coat.

attrs.symptom: Sealed tiles have light patches that look powdery or dull
attrs.cause: Sealer was left to dry on the surface without buffing, leaving a film of residue.
attrs.fix: Apply a small amount of fresh sealer to the affected tile, allow to soften the residue for one minute, then buff immediately with a dry cloth.

attrs.symptom: Milky or streaky appearance after sealing
attrs.cause: Sealer was applied to a floor that still held moisture from washing or from the screed below.
attrs.fix: Strip the sealer with a proprietary stone stripper, allow the floor to dry for at least one week, retest absorbency with a water drop, and reseal.
